utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon everybody. Mr. Registrar, may I ask you to call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is Case number IT-03-66-A, the Prosecutor versus Fatmir Limaj, Haradin Bala and Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Bala if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT BALA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now call for the appearances. For the Prosecution, please -- sorry, you may sit down, Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. With me today are Ms. Shelagh McCall, Ms. Kristina Carey, Ms. Katharina Margetts, and our case manager Mr. Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, and tomorrow we'll be joined in the Prosecution's appeal against Mr. Bala, Mr. Musliu, and Mr. Limaj by Mr. Steffen Wirth, but he cannot join us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Now for the Defence of Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith appearing with Mr. Richard Harvey on behalf of Mr. Bala. We are assisted by our legal assistants Mr. Willemsen and Ms. Buisman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Michael Mansfield and I appear on behalf of Fatmir Limaj, together with my co-counsel Karim Khan. We are also assisted by legal assistant Michelle Butler who sits in the row behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now for Mr. Musliu, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Michael Topolski and together with Steven Powles, we represent Mr. Musliu, also assisted by Ms. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I note that Mr. Musliu and Mr. Limaj are not present. The Appeals Chamber has ordered on 10th May 2007 that should they decide to exercise their right to be present during this appeals hearing as foreseen in Article 21(4)(d) of the Statute of the Tribunal, they shall communicate that intention in writing by the 22nd of May so that appropriate arrangements could be made. I note for the record that neither Mr. Limaj nor Mr. Musliu have informed the Appeals Chamber of such intention. Now, this is the appeal hearing in the case of the Prosecutor against Fatmir Limaj, Haradin Bala, and Isak Musliu. At the outset, I will briefly summarize the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. The appeals deal with crimes committed from May to around the 26th of July, 1998, in the Lapusnik/Llapushnik prison camp and the Berisa/Berisha mountains both situated in central Kosovo, and with the role allegedly played in these events by Limaj, Bala and Musliu, who were members of the Kosovo Liberation Army at the time. Haradin Bala and the Prosecution appeal from a judgement rendered on 30th November 2005 by Trial Chamber II, composed of Judge Parker presiding, and Judges Van Den Wyngaert and Thelin. The Trial Chamber found Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu not guilty on all charges in the indictment and found Haradin Bala guilty on charges of aiding and abetting torture as a violation of the laws and customs of war, Count 4; committing and aiding and abetting cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 6; and committing murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war, Count 10. The Trial Chamber sentenced Haradin Bala to a single sentence of imprisonment of 13 years. The Prosecution appeals the acquittals of Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu and also certain parts of the judgement and the sentence of Haradin Bala. Haradin Bala filed his notice of appeal on 30 December 2005, setting out nine grounds of appeal. On May 2006, he filed his appeal brief and a notice withdrawing the third, fifth, seventh, and ninth ground of appeal. The Prosecution filed its response brief on 19 June 2006. Bala's reply brief was filed on 4 July 2006. The Prosecution filed its notice of appeal on 30 December 2005, and its appeal brief on 15 March 2006. On 27 March 2006, the Prosecution filed a motion for the variation of the notice of appeal pursuant to Rule 108. Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu both filed their response brief on 2nd May 2006 and Bala filed his response brief on 8th May 2006. The Prosecution reply brief was filed on 23rd May 2006. I will now briefly summarize the grounds of appeal. Haradin Bala brings five grounds of appeal. In his first ground of appeal, he alleges that the Trial Chamber incorrectly identified him as the person called "Shala", a prison guard at the Lapusnik/Llapushnik camp. Under his second ground of appeal Haradin Bala submits that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he was present and personally participated in murders committed in the Berisa/Berisha Mountains. In his fourth ground of appeal, Haradin Bala claims that the Trial Chamber erroneously found that he subjected Witness L-12 to cruel treatment. Bala's sixth ground of appeal deals with his alibi defence, which in his submission was erroneously rejected by the Trial Chamber. Finally, in his eighth ground of appeal Haradin Bala argues that the Trial Chamber erroneously found the witnesses L-04 and L-06 credible, resulting in factual errors and a miscarriage of justice. In relation to Haradin Bala, the Prosecution brings two grounds of appeal. In his -- in its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution repeats its challenges of the Trial Chamber's finding in relation to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. In the alternative, in its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in exercising its sentencing discretion by imposing a sentence of 13 years of imprisonment. The Prosecution brings three grounds of appeal in relation to the acquittals of Limaj and Musliu. In its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution challenges the Trial Chamber's application of the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in relation to Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu's personal participation in the Lapusnik prison camp. The Prosecution argues in particular that the Trial Chamber took an erroneously piecemeal approach to the evaluation of the evidence, applying the standard of proof to individual facts that did not have to be proven beyond reasonable doubt. In addition, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber applied a standard of proof that was not beyond a reasonable doubt, but rather one that entertained any doubt, including errors not based upon evidence, logic, and common sense. Under the second ground of appeal, the Prosecution further challenges the application of the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in relation to Fatmir Limaj's and Isak Musliu's position of command and control that included command over Kosovo Liberation Army soldiers in the Lapusnik prison camp. And finally, in the third ground of appeal, the Prosecution challenges the Trial Chamber's finding in relation to the existence of the joint criminal enterprise to ill-treat Serb civilians and perceived Kosovo Albanian collaborators in the Lapusnik prison camp. During this appeals hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation, but I would urge them not just to repeat verbatim or to extensively summarize what is in the briefs. I also wish to note that by a letter of 30 May 2007 the Appeals Chamber has invited the parties to address specific issues during this hearing, issues that do not have to be restated here now. These invitations are made - I want to stress it - without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Appeals Chamber may wish to raise, and in no way constitute an expression of an opinion on the merits of the appeals. I would now like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo, and the appellant must not merely repeat his case from the trial level. Rather, in accordance with Article 25 of the Statute, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. This hearing will proceed according to the scheduling order issued by the Appeals Chamber on 10 May 2007. Counsel for Haradin Bala will present his submissions this afternoon for one hour, 30 minutes. Following a pause, the Prosecution will present its response and afterwards, counsel for Bala will reply. The hearing will then continue tomorrow with the appeal of the Prosecution and the responses from counsel for Limaj and Musliu in accordance with the scheduling order. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Having said this about the manner in which we will proceed today, I would like now to invite counsel for Mr. Bala to present the submissions in support of his appeal. Please, Mr. Guy-Smith, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would be more than happy to do so, Your Honour. Prior to doing so, I'm in a bit of a technical quandary, I have no LiveNote and have been listening to what you have said and trying to hold on to your words but have not been able to view them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can we fix this? Is that okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Bala. Because a centerpiece of the Prosecution against Haradin Bala involved the issue of identification, it is there that I will start. The vagaries of eye-witness identification are well-known, the annals of criminal law are rife with instances of mistaken identification. It's well recognised and an unfortunate reality that the incautious application of eye-witness identification as a basis for conviction has too often resulted in miscarriages of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are terribly sorry, but it is really impossible to hear the counsel properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- This Tribunal in the Kunarac case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, there is a problem. The interpreters are not hearing you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I seem to be having a day of technical difficulty, having been jumping from one courtroom to the next, but I'm sure we will sort it out in a few minutes. Is that better now at this point? Can the interpreters hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is better now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This Tribunal in the Kunarac case has acknowledged that identification evidence is notoriously uncertain. Certainly special caution has been found to be necessary before accepting identification evidence because of the possibility that even a completely honest witness may have been mistaken in their identification. Before going any further, let me pose the following question. Had there been no photo identification evidence submitted and the sole evidence before the Trial Chamber against Haradin Bala had been that a number of witnesses had identified a perpetrator as being 40 to 50, dark hair, with a moustache, generally matching the description of Haradin Bala would the Trial Chamber have entered a conviction? This is a description that probably matches somewhere between 10 and 15 per cent of the people in Kosovo. That is something that I make as a comment. It's not part of the trial record and I don't claim it to be. But had they done so, had the Trial Chamber entered such a conviction, would this Chamber uphold such a conviction? In fact, it is the eye-witness identification that is truly not only the central point, but the only evidence that, in a sense, links him to the charges for which he was convicted. There are no finger-prints, there are no foot-prints, there are no logs, pieces of clothing, photos, or other of objective evidence that identifies Haradin Bala. With this in mind, let us turn to the following as it relates to the identification of Mr. Bala. The Trial Chamber relied on evidence elicited from seven witnesses to determine that Haradin Bala was the same person as the guard called Shala in the prison camp to be found in, I believe, paragraph 632 of the judgement. Those witnesses are Vojko Bakrac, Ivan Bakrac, L-04, L-06, L-10, L-12, and L-96. There is, indeed, also the issue of another witness, that being L-64, however L-64 obtains a different position and will be discussed in a slightly different manner. Of those witnesses, two, L-96 and Ivan Bakrac, were shown photo spreads in which they identified Haradin Bala. With regard to L-96, the Trial Chamber found his evidence, generally speaking, insufficient and suspect standing alone and required corroboration before relying on it. With regard to Ivan Bakrac, the Trial Chamber found, and in that regard they were relying on Exhibit 83, which will become of some moment potentially in our discussion today, Exhibit 83 being a photo spread that was shown in which the likeness of Haradin Bala is good. They found that Ivan Bakrac's identification was one in which there was comfort; however, all by itself, again, the Chamber was not in a position to find that Haradin Bala had been identified as Shala, the prison guard. Three of the witnesses who were shown photo spreads failed to identify him. Of those three, one, the father of Ivan Bakrac, Vojko Bakrac, was unable to identify anyone from the photo spread. The discussion during the judgement was that it was potentially as a result of a poor photographic reproduction. I believe that it is fair to say that the Prosecution in their response brief has taken the position - that would be paragraphs 1.4 through 1.43 - that the photographs that were on the photo spread shown to Vojko Bakrac were exactly as the same as the photographs and the photo spread shown to Ivan Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For the Chamber's assistance, I have copies of the photo spreads and refer the Chamber to the photo spread behind tab 3, which shows the likeness of Haradin Bala in position -- did you get one? Good. I apologise, Ms. Brady. As I was saying, which shows a likeness of Mr. Bala in position at number 8. If the Chamber is to take a look at -- I think we're getting reverse discovery here. If the Chamber is to take a look at the photographic line-up behind tab number 2, you will find Mr. Bala in position number 4, and that is the photographic line-up with which the Trial Chamber indicated that there might be some difficulty because of the poor photographic reproduction. This raises a different issue and an issue that I will deal with when talking about some of the burden-shifting that we contend occurred in this case, but just for the moment, so we have some clarity with regard to the photo line-up that was shown to Ivan Bakrac and to his father, I thought it might be appropriate to take a look at it at this time. With regard to the photo spreads that were shown to L-04 and to L-12 -- if I move over here. I'm having a hard time today. It's okay. With regard to the photographs that were shown to L-04 and L-12, they have been lost, although it was acknowledged and agreed that they were shown photographs -- excuse me, photo spreads and those photo spreads contained a picture of Mr. Bala and there were no identifications. What this does at the outset is that it changes the analysis that the Trial Chamber engaged in from its reliance on seven witnesses who identified Haradin Bala to four immediately. Now, what the Chamber did and where we contend there is a substantial error of law is that with regard to the failed identifications, which is discussed at paragraph 627 of the judgement, the Chamber said it must: "Proceed on the assumption that there was a sufficient likeness and the photographs were of adequate quality to have enabled identification." Well, this statement in and of itself as a basis of which to rely and to proceed, is comforting. However, although this language is language upon which one would believe that the reliance would be such and since there was a failure to identify and, in fact, a negative identification that the Trial Chamber would give weight of some sort to such failure to identify. That is not the case. The Trial Chamber in dealing with assessing the weight to be attached to the failed identifications, wherein they had no line-up to view, said that their failure may also have been dictated by other factors such as lack of certainty and a failure of mistakenly identifying an innocent person or societal pressures. That, again, is language that is found in 627. Now, I suggest, without going any further, just for the moment with regard to the issue of the negative identifications, that in finding that no weight would be attached to them, the Trial Chamber, in fact, shifted the burden to the Defence and that it created a situation whereby those negative identifications which I think we can acknowledge and the decision law acknowledges are equally as important as positive identifications, but here where we have two equally plausible reasons for why the negative identifications existed, one being that they didn't identify the individual because, in fact, Haradin Bala was not the individual; and the other one being, as the Court has suggested, a lack of certainty or fear of mistakenly identifying an innocent person. That their failure to use that which is beneficial in the law as regards to circumstantial evidence in this jurisdiction was error. That error was, unfortunately, compounded by the fact that witnesses were allowed to identify Mr. Bala in court. And in-dock identifications were used with regard to those witnesses who I just referred to, L-04 and L-12, such that the Trial Chamber ultimately came to a position where it relied to some extent, albeit a limited extent we believe, but we are not sure, on in-dock identifications for the purpose of making its ultimate determination of Haradin Bala's involvement and subsequent guilt. Now, in this regard the law is very clear, as set forth in the case of Prosecutor versus Kamuhanda, the appeals judgement, I believe it's paragraph 243, that in-dock identifications are disapproved, shall not be used, and, in fact, are error. Indeed, the Prosecution concedes in its response at paragraph 1.4 that the Trial Chamber erred in relying on such identifications. However -- by suggesting that although the Trial Chamber placed some, and they said albeit little weight on the court ID, such error did not invalidate the decision. Well, what is the situation that we have here? Considering that the conviction of Mr. Bala rests on the collection of seven separate identifications, three of which must be discounted by the decisional law of this Tribunal, the suggestion that at this juncture such reliance on those identifications did not amount to error and did not invalidate the decision is fatally flawed logic in our submission. What occurred - and I take Your Honours admonition with regard to repeating all that was said in the brief - what occurred here was that a series of independently flawed identifications were cobbled together in order to arrive at a conviction. And I suggest to you that this would be similar to a building -- I've thought of a variety of analogies, and I think I'm comfortable with this one at least for the moment, having been living in The Hague where there are many brick houses. If one were to build a wall without any mortar, that wall could not stand. The weakness of the wall is directly related to the fact that it does not have the binding glue to allow for comfort in the strength, and here comfort in the strength of an identification. You could build it high. You could say that a wall, in fact, had been built. But ultimately, leaning up against that wall it would, as I believe the conviction here, necessarily must fall. I'm not engaged, and nor do I suggest that the Chamber engage, in a numbers game with regard to how many positive or negative identifications there may be, but when looking at in an honest sense what occurred here, this Court should be quite suspect and quite uncomfortable with the fact of the collective use of those identifications for purposes of the finding that Haradin Bala was the prison guard known as Shala. Now, some reliance may be placed upon the fact that -- his name, and by that I mean that he had acknowledged that he had a nickname of Shala. There was evidence presented during trial that another individual had the same name. It is conceded, as I speak right now, that that individual was considerably different in stature and form than Haradin Bala. However, the fact that a nickname in and of itself even, if we couple it with those particular attributes of the general description that I had mentioned at the beginning, would not give rise, it is our submission, to a core conviction. I think it's quite important, and this is, perhaps, where there is a marked difference, not only of opinion but of view as to how evidence is analysed here, that the presumption of innocence requires that each fact on which an accused's conviction is based must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The Appeals Chamber has in the case of the Prosecutor versus Ntagerura, Bagambiki and Imanishimwe that if facts are essential -- excuse me, if facts which are essential to a finding of guilt are still doubtful, notwithstanding the support of other facts, this will produce a doubt in the mind of the Trial Chamber that guilt has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Thus, if one of the links is not proved beyond reasonable doubt, the chain will not support a conviction. It is contended that here a number of the links as they related to the identification of Mr. Bala must necessarily fall because three of them were negative, and with regard to the in-dock identifications, those are legally impermissible for purposes of making a determination about the identity of the accused. Before I go any further - and I don't know whether or not your silence means that you have no questions with regard to the issue of identification or not, and I trust that it does. So if that is the case, I will ask if there are any questions with regard to identification, otherwise I will at this point begin to move into another area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Guy-Smith be so careful to switch off the mike that is on his left-hand side -- no, right-hand side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The evidence that was adduced during the trial with regard to Mr. Bala's medical condition or status is uncontroverted. And I think it is important to say that again, uncontroverted, uncontested. The Chamber received evidence from not one but two separate doctors that Mr. Bala suffered from a condition that I will call essentially a heart condition. The gravity of the heart condition is something that was not particularly well explained. Part of that is probably because of the time in which those doctors saw him; however, all recognised that he had had a history of such a condition, that he was arrhythmic, that he was at times, I believe, cyanotic. Meaning that he has poor blood flow and that as a general proposition his health was such that he was advised to not engage in strenuous activities. The reason why this is of importance and the reason why the failure of the Chamber to consider this uncontroverted evidence in the manner that they did, and I do appreciate, of course, that reasonable minds can differ with regard to what an individual can do or with regard to what any particular fact may establish. But in the context of the proceedings against Mr. Bala, there is no doubt that the kinds of activities for which he was charged - and specifically by that I mean the continued beating, I believe it was 59 blows alleged, as well as the journey into the Berisa mountains, a journey that was acknowledged by the Prosecution that a person in good physical health would have difficulty in engaging in - were both physical activities for which the kind of condition that he suffered would make it reasonable, reasonable, that he was not able to engage in these activities. In looking at the standards to be applied, if, as I understand the law here, if there is a version or a question which is open to two inferences, one which is favourable to the defendant which is again a reasonable inference, then the Trial Chamber must adopt such a position. Now, had the evidence been controverted, had there been some contradiction of the medical evidence that was submitted on behalf of Mr. Bala, whereby the issue of his condition itself was in question, we may obtain a different result, we may, although I think that even then there would be some difficulty. But given the fact that the Prosecution chose not to controvert this evidence, the Trial Chamber's finding that his medical condition was too speculative to make a determination, that there was a reasonable inference to be drawn that he was incapable of engaging in the activity for which he was charged, it is our submission was unreasonable and contrary to the law. It has been repeatedly held and certainly it has been held since the time of Tadic that any ambiguity must accrue to the defendant's advantage, and I'm referring the Chamber to the sentencing judgement in Tadic, and that would be paragraph 31. If I could have but a moment. In its decision, the Trial Chamber rely, it is our position, on the only -- on the sole evidence of L-96 to establish that Mr. Bala was present and personally participated in the murders in the Berisa Mountains. The difficulty with this particular holding is twofold. First of all, those witnesses who testified about their trip up the mountain did not positively identify Mr. Bala, and as a matter of fact were not able to identify him from the photo spread. And the Trial Chamber made it quite clear that with regard to the testimony or the evidence of L-96, his evidence is evidence that was highly suspect and would not be given the dignity of any Trial Chamber unless it had been corroborated. L-96 was an individual who was willing to identify an innocent man as being a guard at the camp. L-96 was not uncomfortable in allowing an innocent man to be identified and brought to this Tribunal for prosecution. Fortunately for this young man, there was independent objective evidence that allowed him to go free before the trial began, but for that occurring and the Prosecution's office in that regard can be thanked because they did find such evidence and did - excuse me - and did accept objective evidence, allow him to depart from prosecution. The Trial Chamber said that it had not been prepared to accept and act on the evidence of L-96 alone regarding any material issue and has only given weight to those parts of his evidence which are confirmed in some material particular by other evidence which the Chamber accepts at paragraph 26. He is the only individual who claims that Haradin Bala was at the area which has been identified as the execution site and participated in the killing of the individuals in the Berisa Mountains. There is no, it is our respectful submission, evidence objectively that corroborates or establishes the claim made by L-96, since there are no witnesses who identified in the photo spreads Haradin Bala as the individual who marched up the Berisa Mountains with the -- under his medical condition. We have raised in our appeal grounds concerning the unfair rejection of the alibi defence, and with regard to that issue we rely on what has been written at this time and trust that there is sufficient information and argument there for purposes of the Chamber to make a considered position. Similarly, with regard to the issue concerning L-04 and L-06's statements made to Serbian authorities, we once again rely on the written submissions that were previously made. I believe this brings us to the issue of those questions that the Chamber raised in its letter which I had -- and perhaps I was taking a liberty here or I was misunderstanding something here, which is something that I intended to deal with tomorrow after hearing the Prosecution's appeal because I felt it was more appropriate to deal with it in that manner. But I'm in your hands. It seemed to me that because the issues presented were issues that were, one, contained in the Prosecution's appeal; and two, perhaps more global, that it would be inappropriate for me to jump in beforehand. I'm getting a nod from Ms. Brady. I think that was her understanding, too. I don't know if the Chamber feels differently about this, because when you began your guidance with regard to the structure of argument, you had mentioned those matters. And I'm not sure how you wish to proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, I believe it's up to you to decide when you want to address the issues. You decide the appropriate moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- A moment in which you have the floor, I mean according to the Scheduling Order you can decide when it's appropriate to take up the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since I'll have some more time tomorrow, then I'll be dealing with those issues tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Unless there are any particular questions that the Chamber has at this point, I will at this point stop and attend the argument of my opponent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there are no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That could be either a good thing, a bad thing, or either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So I take your submissions end here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They do for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: For the moment, yeah, sure. Well, we are ahead of our schedule, but I would ask the Prosecutor to start its response now. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I intend to direct my remarks to two grounds of Mr. Bala's appeal. These relate to identification and also to alibi, and these are grounds 1 and 6 of his appeal. My colleague Ms. Carey will be addressing ground 2 of Mr. Bala's appeal, mainly the ground relating to the murders in the Berisa Mountains. She will respond also in the course of that to the submissions made in relation to Mr. Bala's physical condition and the evidence about that condition also relates to ground 4 of the appeal. Unless Your Honours specifically raised any questions, the Prosecution does not intend either to separately address ground 8 in its submissions, and we rely on our response brief in that respect. Before responding to the substantive arguments made on Mr. Bala's behalf, Your Honours, I'd like to clarify the two matters that Mr. Guy-Smith has already tackled. First of all, he is correct to say that the parties agree that the Trial Chamber erred in giving some probative weight to in-court identifications. The parties, however, disagree about the consequences of that. The Defence argues this is an error invalidating the decision and the conviction should be quashed. The Prosecution's position is that in the whole circumstances of this case, it is an error without an impact. The second matter concerning identification relates to the photo-boards shown to Vojko Bakrac. At trial the parties agreed that in 2002 that witness were shown a photo-board on which no one looked familiar to him, that's in the transcript at 1371. The photo-board was admitted into evidence as Exhibit DB1. There were two mistakes made by the parties in agreeing that fact. The first relates to the date in fact Mr. Bakrac was shown the photo-board in 2003; the second is that the exhibit is a copy of the photo-board shown to him, not the original. Again, the parties disagree about the effect of that mistaken agreed fact. The Defence position, as Your Honours have heard, is that in combination with the error over the in-court identifications, this amounts to a miscarriage of justice. The Prosecution's position is that while it is unfortunate that this has happened it has no actual impact on the verdict. Your Honours, this appeal is about whether the Trial Chamber correctly concluded that it has been proved beyond reasonable doubt that Haradin Bala was the perpetrator of the crimes for which he's been convicted. I want, first of all, to ground my submissions about both identification and alibi in a general standard of review and it's this: In order to succeed in his appeal Haradin Bala must show that no reasonable Trial Chamber properly applying the law could have been satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that he was the perpetrator of the crimes; namely, the prison guard Shala. He fails to do so. He argues he should succeed because the Trial Chamber had improperly applied the law on in-court identifications and had there not been a mistake about the Vojko Bakrac photo-board then the failures to identify Mr. Bala on a photo-board by L-04, L-12, and Vojko Bakrac create a reasonable doubt. In fact, in our submission he fails to meet the standard of review and he fails because even with the mistakes made by the Trial Chamber in relation to these two identification matters, no reasonable Trial Chamber would have given such weight to the failures to identify that they would have amounted to a reasonable doubt. They would not have amounted to a reasonable doubt because of the vast body of persuasive evidence which the Trial Chamber accepted all pointing to Haradin Bala being the perpetrator of these crimes. In addition, he fails to meet the standard of review because the Trial Chamber's assessment of his alibi as incredible, incomplete, inconsistent, and unconvincing was perfectly reasonable and is unaffected by the identification mistakes. The Trial Chamber's conclusion was correct that nothing in his alibi and nothing in the evidence about his physical condition, separately or together, raised a reasonable doubt. Your Honours, dealing first with ground 1 relating to identification, in making its decision that Haradin Bala was the perpetrator of these crimes, the Trial Chamber had before it a significant amount of evidence identifying him in different ways, not least of which was that the perpetrator of the crimes, the guard Shala himself said he was Haradin Bala. Bala admits his pseudonym was Shala. He was identified on a photo-board by three different witnesses. All of the victim witnesses gave a similar description of the perpetrator and it matched Haradin Bala. In his submissions, both in his brief and to a large extent today, Mr. Guy-Smith directs the Appeals Chamber's attention only to the evidence of visual identification, and by that the parties mean photo-board identification and in-court identification. The visual identification he argues was insufficient to prove Bala's identity beyond a reasonable doubt, and he founds this argument on the fact that when asked to point the perpetrator out on a photo-board three witnesses failed to do so, L-04, L-12, and Vojko Bakrac. As I understand it his argument in respect of these failures is twofold. Firstly, he argues that the Trial Chamber's decision to give no weight to those failures to identify was an error because unless the Prosecution showed that they failed for some reason other than that the perpetrator's photograph wasn't in the photo-board, then they must raise a reasonable doubt. Second argument, as I understand it, is that in any event in deciding to give no weight to those failures to identify, the Trial Chamber wrongly relied on in-court identifications. Had it not made this error, he argues, these three failures would have cast a reasonable doubt on the identification. Both branches of his argument, in our submission, are without merit. The Prosecution accepts that the Trial Chamber's decision to give weight to the in-court identifications did in some way contribute to its decision not to give weight to the earlier failures to identify by L-04 and L-12. This is clear from a reading of paragraph 631 of the trial judgement. As Mr. Guy-Smith as pointed out, the Trial Chamber talks about seven different people identifying Bala in different ways at different times and the seven is made up of a combination of photo-board and in-court identifications. This photograph, however, is only dealing with visual identification evidence. When one reads this paragraph, in our submission, in light of all of the evidence of identification accepted by the Trial Chamber, it's apparent that the in-court identifications played only a small part in the Trial Chamber's conclusion that there was no reasonable doubt, and their decision would not have been any different had they given the in-court identifications no probative weight whatsoever. In any event, a proper reading of paragraph 631 is that the Trial Chamber used the combination of visual identifications, in-court, and photo-board essentially to eliminate the possibility of honest mistake which it found was inherent in every case of identification. In our submission, it did not mean that the Trial Chamber was not satisfied by individual photo-board identifications, that individual identifications were reliable and credible. It was, in our submission, a safe-guard put in place to protect the accused from the potential flaws of identification evidence. Had the Trial Chamber not used the combination of in-court and photo-board identifications in this way, that is, to eliminate the possibility of honest mistake, it would nonetheless have found that that possibility was eliminated by the other evidence incriminating Haradin Bala and that there was no reasonable doubt about the identification of him. Your Honours, if I may, I'll look a little more closely at just how the Trial Chamber did treat the failures to identify on the photo-board by L-04 and L-12 against their positive in-court identifications. The Trial Chamber deals with the evidence of identification by L-04 and L-12 at paragraph 627 of the judgement. As the Defence correctly points out, the photo-boards shown to those witnesses were not in evidence, which meant the Trial Chamber could not definitively know whether the failure to identify was attributable to the quality of the photograph, and that would clearly be an explanation which would be likely to result in the attribution of no weight to the failure to identify if it were a bad photograph. However, the Trial Chamber recognised that because the photo-boards were missing, to contemplate pure quality as an explanation would be against the presumption of innocence and accordingly the Trial Chamber assumed, in favour of the accused, that the photo-boards were of good quality and that the photograph of Haradin Bala was a sufficient likeness to enable identification. Having made this assumption in his favour, the Trial Chamber expressly stated that the failure to identify: "May well indicate that in their view," that is L-04 and L-12's view, "none of the persons depicted was the man they knew as Shala," that's at 627. It posited against that the possibility that their failure may also have been dictated by other factors, lack of certainty, fear of identifying an innocent person, or societal pressures. There was evidence in general in this case about societal pressure and fear experienced by witnesses and the Trial Chamber referred to that in paragraph 15. In the event, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber does not reach a conclusion about the reason for the failure to identify because of the paucity of evidence about it. The Defence argue that the Prosecution has to eliminate as a possible reason that the perpetrator was not in the line-up, and they argue that because that was not done, the Trial Chamber was obliged to find a reasonable doubt. In our submission, Your Honours, that would only be correct if the failure amounted to a reasonable doubt in the whole circumstances of the case, and you cannot take that failure in isolation. The Prosecution can and did eliminate the possibility that the doubt arising from these failures to identify was reasonable by leading a whole body of credible and reliable evidence, all of which incriminated Haradin Bala. In effect, whatever weight the Trial Chamber might have given to the failures to identify had it not erred in relation to the in-court identifications, the other evidence pointing to Bala was so overwhelming that those failures would never have amounted to a reasonable doubt. In any case, the in-court identifications, although given weight, must have had very little impact on the decision not to attach weight to the failures to identify on the photo-board, and this is apparent from the way in which the Trial Chamber dealt with the process of in-court identifications during the trial itself. For example, Your Honours, the first time an in-court identification was sought by the Prosecution was from Witness L-07 and it was in relation to Fatmir Limaj, that's the transcript 805 to 807. Mr. Limaj's counsel did not object to that process but registered their comment that there was a question as to the weight to be attributed, or the value of an in-court identification. And the Prosecution agreed and the Chamber also took the view that weight was really the issue. In that process of the in-court identification there was a problem because the witness described the colour of tie Mr. Limaj was wearing to identify him in the line-up of three accused and the Presiding Judge interpreted his tie as being a different colour. And there was some confusion and Mr. Limaj's counsel asked him if he would be prepared to stand up to be identified, and that's what happened. Similarly in the evidence of L-07, Mr. Bala's counsel did not object to the in-court identification but made the same comment about weight, and similarly Mr. Bala stood up to be identified. That's in the transcript at 811. In addition to the manner in which the in-court identifications were carried out and whatever weight they were going to be worth based on that process, the Trial Chamber made it clear that the in-court identifications were being treated with a great deal of caution, confirming that they were carrying very little weight. In paragraph 627 of the judgement, it's clear the Trial Chamber considered there to be a number of dangers in accepting in-court identification by these witnesses, not least because they'd seen television coverage of the proceedings and that was something throughout the case that caused this Trial Chamber some disquiet with respect to subsequent identifications. The Trial Chamber's conclusion was that it: "Must approach the in-court identifications by each of L-04 and L-12 with a clear recognition that each could be mistaken." Thus, in our submission, although the in-court identifications were given weight by the Trial Chamber, it was extremely limited and was certainly not such as to suggest that the in-court identifications were a significant reason for disregarding the earlier failures to identify. Your Honours, in relation to Vojko Bakrac, he was not asked to make an in-court identification, so the process in respect of him was a little different. The Trial Chamber dealt with his failure to identify on a photo-board at paragraph 604 of the judgement. That paragraph, in our submission, demonstrates that the fact that Exhibit DB1 was a copy of the photo-board, not the original, was not significant. The Trial Chamber noted that it didn't know whether this was the original photo-board or a copy and so it could not reach a view about the reason for failure, so it did not assume a bad-quality photograph as the reason. On the other hand, however, in favour of the accused it noted clearly that because of this failure, reference by Vojko Bakrac and other witnesses to Shala may not be references to Haradin Bala. Thus, it gave weight to Vojko Bakrac's failure to identify to the extent that it was not prepared to neutralise it and it weighed it into the mix of the whole of the evidence. In our submission, this also demonstrates that the Trial Chamber was cognizant of Professor Wagenaar's testimony, that failures to identify might, in principle, be significant and should not simply be dismissed. That's the transcript, 7223 to 7224. Your Honours, it would be a mistake to read the identification analysis by the Trial Chamber in relation to Haradin Bala in isolation of the whole judgement. Because the Trial Chamber set out its approach to identification evidence at the beginning of the judgement. At paragraph 20 it stated: "It is the cumulative effect of the evidence, that is, the totality of evidence bearing on the identification of an accused which must be weighed to determine whether the Prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that each accused is a perpetrator as alleged." Bearing that approach in mind when one reads the section entitled: "Was Haradin Bala identified at the Llapushnik prison camp?" That's paragraph 603 to 633, it's clear in finding the identity of the perpetrator to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, the Trial Chamber did not rely to any great extent on the in-court identifications. It did not rely solely on visual identifications. In fact, the Trial Chamber noted in its judgement at paragraph 20 that visual identifications are: "But one piece of what may be the relevant evidence." In deciding that the perpetrator's identity was proved beyond a reasonable doubt, the Trial Chamber relied on a tapestry of evidence other than visual identification, all of which pointed to Haradin Bala. Firstly, the Trial Chamber considered the evidence given by the witnesses who were detained at the camp about the treatment they received at the hands of the guard Shala. Each gave a physical description. They described his functions and his role in the camp. They all gave evidence that he had the pseudonym Shala. Having examined that body of evidence, the Trial Chamber was firstly satisfied that all the victim witnesses were talking about the same person. That's at paragraph 621. The real issue, Your Honours, for the Trial Chamber was whether it was proved beyond reasonable doubt that that person was Haradin Bala. Witnesses gave, as Your Honours have heard, a physical description of Shala, his age, his height, his hair, his bad teeth, his moustache. The Trial Chamber made a finding that the descriptions matched the appearance of Haradin Bala, that's at 621, and in particular - and this is where I would disagree with what Mr. Guy-Smith said about a general description matching a percentage of the population - some of the features of the description in the context of this case held more significance than otherwise might have been so. In particular, the witness described Shala as being in his 40s or 50s. This was of greater significance than one might normally expect in this case because it was unusual to have a KLA soldier of that age, and the majority of the soldiers were much younger than that and Bala was in his earlier 40s at the material time. Your Honours, the descriptions pointed to Haradin Bala. It was not disputed by Bala that his pseudonym was Shala and that he was in the KLA. There was further evidence about those facts from people who knew him, Dr. Zeqir Gashi had known him for 10 to 15 years before the war and testified at 5621 to 5623 that Bala was a KLA soldier in Lapusnik and that he was using the pseudonym Shala. Ruzdhi Karpuzi, another KLA soldier whose pseudonym was also Shala, gave evidence that he shared that pseudonym with Haradin Bala, that's transcript 3139. Of course, none of this evidence necessarily connected Bala with the prison guard Shala. That connection was proved beyond reasonable doubt by two strands of evidence. The evidence established, first of all, that there were two KLA soldiers named Shala in Lapusnik at the material time, that's trial judgement 622. These were Haradin Bala and Ruzdhi Karpuzi. The Prosecution eliminated any possibility that Ruzdhi Karpuzi was the guard Shala. This was done through a variety of sources of evidence. Firstly, Karpuzi gave evidence of his duties in the KLA, and they were principally observation of a Serb check-point. He also gave evidence that he had not been in the buildings used as the prison camp, that's transcript 3085-3093. Secondly, L-64, another KLA soldier, said the guards at the prison were Haradin Bala and a soldier named Murrizi. That's transcript 4444 to 4445. Thirdly, the description of the guard Shala did not match Ruzdhi Karpuzi. Karpuzi was eight years younger, 15 centimetres taller. Karpuzi had no moustache, and finally Karpuzi walked with an obvious limp. That's in the trial judgement at 622. The second strand of evidence sealing the connection between Haradin Bala and the guard Shala was the evidence of L-07, one of the victim witnesses. He testified that he met Shala at a petrol station in 1999, the year after the crimes, and when he greeted him as Shala, the guard replied, "My real name is Haradin Bala." That's transcript 810. The perpetrator of these crimes himself said his name is Haradin Bala. From paragraph 625 of the judgement, it's clear this was a compelling piece of evidence accepted without qualification by the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, in our submission this overwhelming body of evidence is unaffected by the error relating to in-court identifications. It directly incriminated Haradin Bala. It ruled out the only other Shala in Lapusnik. It did not point to anyone else. Your Honours, were that not enough in itself, the Trial Chamber had before it the visual identification evidence that you've heard about, and in our submission, the visual identifications by photo-board are similarly unaffected by the error in relation to the in-court identification. The Defence refers only to two photo-board identifications, those by Ivan Bakrac and L-96. Of course, Bala was also identified on a photo-board by L-64 - that's in the transcript at 4454 - but the Prosecution accepts that the principal identifications it relies on are those of Ivan Bakrac and L-96. The Defence argues that the Trial Chamber conceded there were flaws in both of the identifications by Ivan Bakrac and L-96 and he refers to a general reservation about the evidence of L-96 on the part of the Trial Chamber. In our submission, this argument misrepresents the Trial Chamber's view of the photo-board identification by Ivan Bakrac and it fails to recognise the inherent credibility of the identification by L-96 and that any concerns about the content of his testimony generally could have been assuaged by the act of identification itself. Your Honours, dealing first with Ivan Bakrac. Contrary to what the Defence suggest, in our submission the Trial Chamber had no hesitation about Ivan Bakrac's credibility and reliability, including in relation to his photo-board identification of Haradin Bala. At paragraph 624 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber comments that the identification by Ivan Bakrac stands out because of the Trial Chamber's favourable assessment of his evidence in general and because of the "care, honesty, competence, and [in relation to identification as in most matters] the reliability he displayed." In stating that view which, in our submission, amounts to a clear acceptance of the credibility and reliability of Ivan Bakrac's identification, the Trial Chamber reiterated the extensive opportunity this young man had to view Shala. Shala had been generally respectful to him and his father. He had played chess with Shala. In addition, the Trial Chamber held that his identification was immediate and unhesitating. The Trial Chamber weighed the expert evidence of Professor Wagenaar about the dangers of photo-board identification and determined that this did not in any way detract from the unhesitating and confident identification by Ivan Bakrac. It accepted his identification and in the paragraph of the judgement dealing with that it expressed no reservation about its acceptance. Now, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber may have been able to rely on this identification alone, however exercising caution only to the benefit of the accused, what it did do is recognise in a general sense the inherent possibility of honest mistake in every identification case. The Trial Chamber dealt with this at length in paragraph 17 of the trial judgement. Its decision to guard against such mistake by choosing not to rely on a single identification was in no way, in our submission, an indication that it did not unequivocally accept the identification by Ivan Bakrac. They were simply putting a safe-guard in place to protect the accused. In our submission, that safe-guard was met by the tapestry of evidence referred to already, both circumstantial and direct, but it was also met by the two further photo-board identifications, principally L-96, and though we place less significance on it, L-64. Your Honours, L-96 recognised Haradin Bala on the photo-board immediately. In its brief, the Defence criticises the Trial Chamber's acceptance of this identification because the procedure was not correctly followed. They argued the same at trial, but any faults in that procedure happened after L-96 had picked Bala out of the photo-board. At paragraph 613, the Trial Chamber fully considered the procedure that was undertaken and held that the identification was not affected by any shortcomings. In our submission, the Defence have not shown why the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to come to that view. The second criticism, Your Honours, is that the Trial Chamber should not have accepted the identification by L-96 without corroboration, which it had required in general for his testimony. In his brief, and again today, Bala argues that L-96 was not corroborated because the Trial Chamber did not find Ivan Bakrac's identification to be without flaw. But in our submission, when one reads properly the Trial Chamber's assessment of Ivan Bakrac's identification, it's clear that it was not flawed and it was accepted without reservation. L-96 was corroborated by Ivan Bakrac. He was also corroborated by the evidence of L-07 that Shala himself admitted to being Haradin Bala. And he was corroborated by the circumstantial evidence, all pointing to Bala that I've already set out. In any event, in our submission, whatever the hesitation the Trial Chamber may have had about the candour of L-96 in general, what is indisputable that when confronted with a photo-board of eight pictures all matching the description he had given of Shala, L-96 immediately picked Haradin Bala's photograph. There was evidence that he had not seen Bala on television or in pictures before doing so - that's the transcript 2396 - he had not seen Shala since his escape from the Berisa mountains, that's the same transcript reference. That process in itself could have been taken by the Trial Chamber as eliminating concern about L-96's credibility. The credibility issue does not impact on the process of identification by photo-board. The exercise of identifying a perpetrator from a photo-board is the point at which lack of credibility is exposed precisely because it is outwith the control of the witness, outwith the control of L-96 and yet it was Haradin Bala's photograph he picked out and he picked it immediately. By requiring further corroboration, the Trial Chamber had been cautious and this was to the benefit of the accused and the identification was properly corroborated. To sum up in relation to identification, Your Honours, Mr. Bala's challenge to the judgement essentially in our submission comes down to this: He complains that the Trial Chamber's decision not to give weight to the failures to identify by L-04 and L-12 and Vojko Bakrac amounted to a reasonable doubt and if the Trial Chamber had not given weight to the in-court identifications, it would have found a reasonable doubt. In making that submission, in our view he encourages this Chamber to view only the visual identification in isolation of the whole picture. That, in our submission, is an entirely artificial exercise, and if Trial Chambers were to engage in it, it would prevent them from cross-checking pieces of evidence against other evidence that they accept, which is a fundamental part of the process of determining whether a case is proved beyond reasonable doubt. In our submission, when one examined the totality of evidence incriminating Haradin Bala, he has failed to show that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have found it proved beyond reasonable doubt that he was the perpetrator of crimes for which he's been convicted. Indeed, whatever weight would have been placed by the Trial Chamber on the failures to identify, had it disregarded the in-court identifications, given its other findings, the Trial Chamber would have come to the same conclusion that there was no reasonable doubt that Haradin Bala was the guard Shala. Accordingly, in our submission, ground 1 should be dismissed. Your Honours, I'm conscious of the time and I will probably take more than ten minutes. I don't know whether the Bench wishes to rise early or whether I should begin my discussion of alibi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You can go on. There are no questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You can go on for ten minutes and then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to ground 6, that is the ground relating to the Trial Chamber's treatment of Mr. Bala's alibi, of course, the Prosecution accepts alibi is not a defence. What is required is that even given evidence of an alibi the Prosecution proves its case beyond a reasonable doubt. This Chamber in the Celebici trial judgement at 581 expressed that it this way that the accused must be acquitted if there is a reasonable possibility that the alibi is true. In deciding whether Haradin Bala was identified beyond a reasonable doubt, the Trial Chamber weighed all OF the evidence for and against him, including that relating to his alibi and including that relating to his physical condition. And those aspects are dealt with at paragraphs 634 to 650 of the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber assessed the evidence supporting the alibi and in relation to the physical condition and found it incomplete, inconsistent, and ultimately unconvincing. The Defence argues an error of law in respect of this ground, and it is a common theme in their appeal, in our submission, namely that the Trial Chamber reversed the burden of proof and in this ground required him to prove that his alibi was consistent and credible, not just plausible and that the Trial Chamber made an adverse finding in relation to his alibi because he did not give sworn testimony. Your Honours, there was no error in the way the Trial Chamber dealt with the alibi. Dealing, first of all, with the reversal of the burden of proof, in his brief Mr. Bala transforms the test that the alibi must be a reasonable possibility into one that requires him only to produce a plausible alibi and one might pause to consider whether plausibility necessarily encompasses the concept of reasonableness nonetheless, having assessed all of the identification evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: -- the Trial Chamber expressly stated that before reaching its ultimate finding --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel kindly slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Could you slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Having assessed all the identification evidence, the Trial Chamber expressly stated that before reaching its ultimate finding on the question of identification, it would weigh those two further issues, the alibi and the physical condition, that's at paragraph 633. In our submission, this was the correct approach for the Trial Chamber to take; namely, to see whether in light of all of the evidence in the case, both for and against, anything in the evidence raised a reasonable doubt. The order in which the Trial Chamber carried out the analysis of the evidence demonstrates, in our submission, that it did not reverse the burden of proof. That is, it looked first of all at the Prosecution evidence to see if it could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, and then having decided that the Prosecution case met that level, it considered the Defence evidence of alibi and physical condition to see if that contained a reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber in doing this will obviously have had in mind any doubt remaining after the Prosecution case, albeit by themselves they may not have risen to the level of reasonableness required for an acquittal. But to conduct the analysis of evidence in this way meant that the Trial Chamber left open until the very end the possibility that, cumulatively, a reasonable doubt might arise from the evidence that was led for and against. Having considered all of the evidence, the Trial Chamber concluded at 650 that it was not left with a reasonable doubt, despite the alibi advanced and despite the evidence about the health of Mr. Bala. There is no indication, in our submission, from the Trial Chamber's analysis or the way in which it expressed its conclusion that it required Bala to prove his alibi. It did not reverse the burden of proof. Moving on to the second argument that Mr. Bala makes in relation to his failure to testify and what he says the Trial Chamber made of that, he argues that the Trial Chamber in dismissing his alibi evidence was effectively drawing an adverse inference from his decision not to give sworn testimony. In our submission, this is really a complaint about the way in which the Trial Chamber used Bala's unsworn statement. He argues in his brief that it was not evidence, it should not have been used to assess the credibility and the reliability of his alibi witnesses, and in any event it was unfair to use it against him because it was incomplete and lacking in detail. Your Honours, Mr. Bala conducted his defence on the basis of an alibi and he cannot remedy on appeal the failure to make a comprehensive unsworn statement. An unsworn statement is evidence in this Tribunal and under Rule 84 the Trial Chamber is entitled to give it what weight it considers appropriate. The Defence have not articulated why the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to treat his unsworn statement in the way it did. The fact that his alibi was ultimately found not to have a consistent and credible basis does not mean that the Trial Chamber made an adverse finding because of his failure to identify; it simply highlighted the lack of solid foundation provided by his unsworn statement which Bala himself acknowledges was incomplete and lacking in detail. The Trial Chamber did not err in this respect. Your Honours, that may be a convenient moment in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, if it's convenient for you, I think we can break now for half an hour and we continue at 6.30 -- 4.30, sorry, 16.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we'll resume our hearing, and I give the floor to the Prosecution to continue its submission. You have the floor, Ms. McCall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, before the break I was discussing Mr. Bala's ground of appeal in relation to his alibi and I dealt with his argument that the Trial Chamber reversed the burden of proof and his argument about the way in which the Trial Chamber dealt with his unsworn statement. In his brief he points out that the Trial Chamber stated in the judgement that the testimony of the alibi witnesses does not necessarily negate the evidence that Bala remained in Lapusnik. He argues that this shows that the Trial Chamber required him to prove his alibi. While that may be clumsily phrased, in our submission, read in context, the Trial Chamber did no such thing. In fact, as with the identification evidence, in our submission, the Trial Chamber made a careful and thorough assessment of the credibility and reliability of the alibi witnesses, and it set out that assessment in its judgement at paragraphs 634 to 647. Both parties in their written submissions have made specific arguments in relation to the evidence. I don't intend to rehearse those here but Your Honour will find the Prosecution discussion of the evidence in chapter 4 of the response brief parts E and D, that's pages 43 to 56. In our submission, when one reviews the way the Trial Chamber conducted its analysis of that evidence, just as when one reviews the analysis of the evidence relating to identification, in our submission the Defence have not shown why the Trial Chamber's assessments of credibility and reliability were unreasonable. He has not shown any error in the manner in which the Trial Chamber dealt with his alibi. In our submission he simply disagrees with the Trial Chamber and their conclusion that any possibility that Bala was not the guard Shala was not a reasonable one. With the benefit of the breaks, Your Honour, I intend to curtail my submissions at that point and invite the Chamber to dismiss ground 6. I'm happy to answer any questions in relation to this ground. If there are no questions, I will hand over to my colleague Ms. Carey, who will address ground 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. So you can move to the other grounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am going to be addressing ground 2, relating to Haradin Bala's presence and participation in the Berisa Mountain murders. In three subgrounds, the Defence alleges that no reasonable Trial Chamber, properly applying the law, could find beyond a reasonable doubt that Bala was physically capable of participating in the Berisa Mountain march, that he did not turn away before reaching the killing site, and that he did not shoot. The Prosecution submits that the findings of the Trial Chamber are correct and supported by ample, credible, and reliable evidence. I am going to address the subgrounds and subsections in the order in which they appear in the briefs. Although I will not be addressing ground 4 relating to Bala's physical capacity to engage in the beating of Witness L-12 in any real detail, the deficiencies of the Defence argument in the second ground of appeal are equally apparent in the fourth ground of appeal. The Defence fails to address itself to the findings of the Trial Chamber and it fails to demonstrate how evaluating the totality of the evidence, its findings were unreasonable. Now, there are two common themes that are woven through the Defence subgrounds. First, the Defence asked this Chamber to stand in the place of the Trial Chamber and consider the evidence as if this were a trial de novo. In each submission, the Defence sets out the evidence that it feels is relevant and seeks to have this Chamber make its own determination as to whether or not this evidence raises a reasonable doubt. In so doing, the Defence fails to meet the standard on appeal, which is to show that no reasonable Trial Chamber, properly applying the law, could have been satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Bala was present in the Berisa Mountains and participated in the murder of nine prisoners. Second, the Defence seeks to have this Chamber compartmentalise select pieces or strands of evidence for individual analysis rather than to consider the evidence as a whole. This approach is -- was clearly articulated in paragraphs 40 through 42 of the Defence reply brief, where the Defence insists that the health evidence should have been considered in isolation from the witnesses' identification of Mr. Bala or the evidence relating to the physical condition of the prisoners who marched into the Berisa Mountains. This isolate-and-negate strategy creates the impression that the evidence which is identified by the Defence raises a reasonable doubt, when in fact it does not. The Trial Chamber's conclusions regarding Bala's participation were reasonable in light of the entire body of evidence. The Defence's first ground of appeal illustrates both of these themes. The Defence argues that the evidence of his physical condition raised a reasonable doubt that he was present in the Berisa Mountains. After paying lip-service to the deference which must be afforded to the Trial Chamber's evaluation of the evidence in paragraph 136 of its appeal brief, in paragraphs 137 through 144, the Defence then invites the Appeals Chamber to consider the evidence anew. In this exercise, however, the Defence would have this Chamber ignore the various strands of evidence that were considered by the Trial Chamber and base its own evaluation upon a single evidentiary thread: The medical evidence. The Trial Chamber was required, however, to consider all of the evidence relating to this issue and to determine, first, whether the Prosecution's evidence could prove Bala's participation beyond a reasonable doubt; and second, whether the evidence relating to Bala's alibi or physical condition raised a reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber correctly found that the evidence, in its totality, established Bala's presence and participation beyond a reasonable doubt. In reaching its conclusion, the Trial Chamber considered the following strands of evidence, the references for which can be found in paragraphs 447 through 457 of the judgement and in paragraphs 2.2 through 2.4 of the Prosecution's response brief. First, the Trial Chamber considered the direct testimony of five witnesses that the guard called Shala had participated in their imprisonment in the Lapusnik camp. These witnesses testified that it was this Shala from the camp that accompanied them on the 26th of July, 1998, into the Berisa Mountains. Their evidence was that during the Serb offensive on that day, Shala and Murrizi gathered the prisoners together and marched them to the Berisa Mountains. During that march this same guard Shala, together with Murrizi, divided the group and then released one group and then this same guard Shala and Murrizi and possibly a third KLA soldier marched the second group of prisoners to a clearing in the woods where they murdered nine of them. The Trial Chamber also found that the guard Shala in the camp and in the Berisa Mountains was Haradin Bala. This has been covered in some detail in the submissions of my colleague, Ms. McCall, relating to identification so I will not reiterate those arguments here. The Defence argues that despite this direct evidence, the evidence of his heart condition still raised a reasonable doubt that he was present. This argument, however, ignores the findings regarding the conditions of the march and the condition of the other persons participating in the march. When these findings are considered with the direct evidence of the five witnesses who said that Bala, the guard Shala, was with them on the march, it is clear that the evidence of Bala's health did not raise reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber's findings and supporting references concerning the conditions of the march and the conditions of the participants can be found in paragraphs 447 through 457 of the judgement, and I will just summarize them for you. The 26th of July, 1998, was a hot day. The witnesses described the path as difficult. The total march was approximately 4 kilometres in distance. The first part of that march, which was principally uphill, took 40 minutes; it was followed by a rest break of approximately two hours. The following portion of the march with the second group of prisoners was both up and downhill and was interrupted by another rest break. The group of prisoners that were undertaking the march included persons who had been imprisoned for as long as six weeks, chained to a wall in a stifling damp room, with an overflowing bucket of human excrement that functioned as the prisoners' only toilet. Some of these prisoners were elderly. Several had been badly beaten during the course of their detention and had wounds that included broken ribs and a broken sternum. One prisoner had a broken leg, and this necessitated that other prisoners support or carry him throughout the march. None of these prisoners had eaten in three to four days. The totality of the evidence demonstrates that Bala was one of the KLA soldiers, herding this group of mainly exhausted and physically debilitated prisoners into the Berisa mountains. Evidence of Bala's health condition, when considered together with this evidence, does not raise a reasonable doubt as to the fact that he was there. Now, in its error of law, the second part of the first subground, the Defence argues that the Trial Chamber shifted the burden of proof by making the Defence prove that Bala's physical incapacity -- to make the Defence prove Bala's physical incapacity beyond a reasonable doubt. The logical outcome of the Defence's argument in this subsection would be that once the Defence has put forward any evidence, the evidence therefore constitutes a reasonable doubt, unless the Prosecution specifically demonstrates that this evidence is incredible or unreliable. This is simply incorrect. The Trial Chamber's analysis of this evidence was proper. It first considered whether the Prosecution had led evidence that was capable of proving its case beyond a reasonable doubt, and it then assessed whether there was credible and reliable evidence in the record that created a reasonable doubt. It assessed the medical evidence and concluded, in light of the fact that five witnesses identified Shala, who was also identified as Bala on the march, and in light of the fact that the medical evidence did not demonstrate that Bala could not have been present, that no reasonable doubt existed. The Defence, therefore, fails to show how no reasonable Trial Chamber properly applying the law could have been satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt as to Bala's participation and presence in the Berisa Mountains. This was, in fact, the only reasonable conclusion available to the Trial Chamber because the medical evidence, at best, only demonstrated that strenuous exercise was medically inadvisable. In paragraphs 648 and 649, the Trial Chamber considered the following medical evidence. It found in paragraph 648, that Bala suffered from angina, high blood pressure, and an irregular heart beat. Accordingly, Bala was advised to limit himself to light physical activity, to avoid overexertion. However, the Trial Chamber also found in paragraph 648, that despite the fact that Bala "had experienced a blood pressure problem and an arrhythmic heart beat since before 1998" he nevertheless "joined the KLA." It also found that "while for much of the time Bala was engaged in lighter duties, during his KLA service he also participated in actual military action." This led the Trial Chamber to conclude that despite his physical condition Bala was able to engage in the demanding physical activities of combat or that he did not always hold back from physical demands of KLA service because of his physical condition. The Defence has responded in its reply brief, that although the two doctors did not testify that Bala was physically incapable of undertaking the Berisa march, their evidence was sufficiently compelling to raise reasonable doubt. In paragraph 149 of its appeal brief, the Defence asserts that Dr. Zaqir Gashi stated: "It could not have been possible for a person who suffers from serious vascular condition to engage in strenuous physical exercise." Dr. Gashi, however, was not presented with any of the specifics of this particular journey, such as its distance; its degree of elevation, gain, and loss; the time allotted for the journey; and the number and frequency and length of the rest breaks, nor was he presented with the condition of the other participants. Although the Defence argues in paragraph 35 of its reply brief that these additional facts are irrelevant, absent these specific facts, Dr. Gashi's opinion is wholly hypothetical and cannot support the inference --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker speak more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: I apologise to the translators. Dr. Gashi's opinion is wholly hypothetical and cannot support the inference suggested by the Defence. Although the Defence makes much of the fact that the medical evidence was not contested, this is irrelevant. The medical evidence demonstrated only that Bala had a heart condition and that strenuous exercise was inadvisable. The Trial Chamber, on the other hand, before -- on the other hand, had before it the direct evidence of Shala's participation in the march, the identification of Bala as Shala, the evidence relating to the nature of the march, and the condition of the participants, as well as the medical evidence relating to Bala's heart condition. This evidence, when evaluated as a whole, as is required, leaves no reasonable doubt that Bala participated in the march into the Berisa Mountains. The Defence has failed to demonstrate that the Trial Chamber's conclusion was the one that no reasonable Trial Chamber, properly applying the law, could have reached. The Prosecution notes that while it has not addressed itself to the Defence's fourth ground of appeal, relating to Bala's physical capacity to engage in the beating of L-12 in the prison camp, the Defence arguments in that ground suffer from the same logical flaws. In the fourth ground, the Defence argues that the evidence of Bala's physical condition raised reasonable doubt about Bala's ability to beat Witness L-12 with a stick for a sustained period of time.
