As in the first subground, the Defence argument ignores the direct testimony of both the victim, L-12 and L-04, the prisoner chained next to L-12, who identified the guard Shala as the beater. The Defence similarly overstates the medical evidence on this point as neither medical witness was willing to comment on Bala's physical ability to beat a person over a sustained period. Accordingly, this fourth ground of appeal should also be dismissed. I'll turn now to the second and third subgrounds of appeal. In its second and third subgrounds the Defence argues that the Chamber failed to give effect to two inferences that are consistent with innocence: Namely, that Bala was not present at the killing site and that Bala did not physical participate in the killings. With respect to this third subground of appeal, although they are closely linked, the Prosecution seeks to rest on its written submissions in the brief and I will only be addressing the second subground of appeal. The inference that Bala was not present or turned away from the killing site was not an inference available to the Trial Chamber in light of the direct evidence of L-96 which was corroborated in material respects by other reliable and credible evidence. This is an example of, again, that isolate-and-negate strategy that was employed in the first subground where the Defence addresses just a single piece or strand of evidence as if it is the only evidence that the Trial Chamber should have considered. The Defence states that there were two categories of evidence relating to what occurred at the killing site in the Berisa Mountains: The testimony of L-96 and the ballistics and forensic reports. According to the Defence, L-96's evidence is uncorroborated, therefore it must be excluded. Once L-96's evidence is excluded, the Defence goes on to argue, the Trial Chamber was left with only the ballistics and forensics reports, which were insufficient to establish Bala's guilt because they do not independently exclude the reasonable inference that Bala was not present at the killing site. Now, first, I'd like to take the opportunity to address one of Mr. Guy-Smith's points regarding L-96's credibility that was made in his submissions. L-96 never identified Agim Murtezi in a photo-board and you can find this in the transcript at 2371. L-96 gave evidence that he learned second-hand that Murrizi's, the other KLA guard, real name was Agim Murtezi. You can find this at transcript pages 2509 and 2510. The same Defence arguments that you heard were canvassed at trial and the record is clear that L-96 never identified Agim Murtezi in the manner that was suggested by Mr. Guy-Smith. The Defence's summary exclusion of L-96's direct evidence ignores the fact that it was corroborated in material respects by both the other evidence that the Defence does identify, namely, the ballistics and forensic reports, and by a large quantity of other reliable evidence that was accepted by the Trial Chamber and which the Defence simply fails to acknowledge or address. The Trial Chamber in paragraph 451 correctly relied upon L-96's direct evidence about Bala's presence and participation in the Berisa Mountains. L-96 testified as to the following facts about the events at the killing site: That Bala directed the march of the second group of prisoners to a clearing and ordered the group to sit down; Bala then joined Murrizi and a third soldier, stated, "This is your death penalty," and charged his Kalashnikov; L-96 also testified that he heard bursts of fire coming from two Kalashnikovs. Each one of these references can be found in the judgement at paragraph 451. The Trial Chamber was very careful with L-96's testimony throughout the judgement. It only relied upon this testimony because the Chamber found that it was significantly corroborated by independent evidence from witnesses L-10, L-04, L-06, and L-12, as well as by the ballistics and forensic reports. The following evidence is discussed at length in paragraphs 447 through 457 of the judgement, that multiple witnesses testified to Bala's critical role in directing the march, that he ordered them to form a line holding hands, that he gave instructions to Murrizi as to which paths to follow, that he divided the prisoners into two groups at the cherry tree, and issued the release papers freeing the first group. These same witnesses saw Bala walk back in the direction of the second group, a group which included L-96 and the nine persons whose bodies were found at the killing site. The Trial Chamber also took note of the fact that L-96 was able to lead investigators to the grave-site and that the bodies of the nine persons identified by L-96 and witnesses in the first group were positively identified in the forensic report. It also took note of the fact that cartridges and bullets from two separate Kalashnikovs were found at the killing site. In the evidence cited in paragraphs 448 and 456 of the judgement, L-96 testified that Bala and a third soldier had a Kalashnikov and Murrizi had an M-48 rifle. L-10 testified that Bala and a third soldier carried an automatic weapon and that Murrizi had a rifle. L-04 stated that Bala always carried an automatic weapon. Although the Trial Chamber mistakenly identifies Bala and Murrizi as having a Kalashnikov, this statement is not founded in the evidence cited by the Trial Chamber. Despite this mistake, it is clear that the Trial Chamber's ultimate findings in paragraphs 453 and 454 are amply supported by the evidence. When one considers the direct testimony of L-96 and the supporting fabric of the corroborating independent evidence, there was no evidential basis from which the Trial Chamber could reasonably infer that Bala turned away before the killing site. All of the evidence on the record supports the opposite conclusion. There is no evidence that Bala turned away. The inference that the Defence asks you to draw is wholly speculative. Therefore, the Defence has failed to show how no reasonable Trial Chamber properly applying the law could have been satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Bala was not present at the killing site and this subground must be rejected. As I mentioned earlier, with respect to the third subground, the Prosecution is going to rest on its written submissions. Therefore, in conclusion, for the reasons set out in the Prosecution's response brief and in the submissions of myself and my colleague Ms. McCall, the Prosecution submits that all of Bala's grounds of appeal should be dismissed. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm available for questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Is this concluding the submissions of the Prosecution? Well, if that's the case, I turn to the appellant and for the reply. You have the floor, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I wish to start with the issue of L-96. L-96, we submit, was a liar. An individual who, when confronted with the fact that he was willing to accuse an innocent man of serious and, indeed, horrible crimes, indicated that he had seen him on television. And when asked whether or not he would apologise to that man in this very courtroom at that very seat, indicated that he refused to do so. L-96 is the only person who claims that Haradin Bala was at the Berisa Mountain execution site. Now, interestingly what has just occurred is that the Prosecution has suggested that a number of individuals, that's L-04, L-10 -- I'm sorry, L-04, L-12, L-06, and L-10 all testified that Haradin Bala was present on the trip from the camp up through the Berisa Mountains. That is inaccurate. Shala was the individual, and Shala is what this fight is all about: Whether or not Haradin Bala was correctly identified as the guard Shala. This is what we have. I said it before and I'll say it again. L-04 and L-12 made negative identifications in a photo spread that was given no weight. L-06 and L-10 identified Haradin Bala in court, that is conceded error. I question whether or not, based on that evidence, a reasonable Trial Chamber, properly applying the law, would find that Haradin Bala was identified as the individual Shala who walked up the Berisa Mountains, without giving any impact whatsoever to the issue of his medical condition. I'm reminded, because in large measure what we're dealing with here is the application of this test of drawing inferences, circumstantial evidence, and it's very clear that it is not sufficient that a finding is reasonable conclusion available from that evidence if it is possible for another conclusion to be found. Specifically, the Appeals Chamber in Celebici stated: "If there is another conclusion which is also reasonably open from the evidence and which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted." With regard to the issue of Mr. Bala's physical condition, once again, uncontested. I ask you whether or not there was a reasonable inference consistent with innocence that could be drawn from this evidence. Was there a reasonable inference that Haradin Bala's physical condition precluded him from performing the activities that Shala so performed, independent of the issue of the identification? And I suggest to you the answer is yes. I am very troubled by what I think has occurred here in terms of the identification conclusions, and specifically the language that we have been discussing in the judgement, and that's at paragraph 627, and I think there's no doubt what happened. Having made a determination they were not in a position to make findings with regard to negative identifications, they were discounted. And then the Trial Chamber, in summing up the identification evidence at paragraph 631 said the following: "While no one of the separate" -- let's start that at the beginning. "While no one of the seven separate identifications, when considered separately, would satisfy the Chamber that Shala is Haradin Bala because of the various possibilities for honest mistake identified earlier, in the particular circumstances now being considered," and this is where I wish to focus for the moment, "the combination of these particular seven separate identifications does in the Chamber's finding negate the possibilities of mistake." Well, three of them were negative; the balance of them were in court; two forms of identification which are either directly disapproved of or strongly suspect; and we are left with the identification of L-96 - who reminds me of an old adage, falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus - and one other. To cobble together a conviction based on this kind of identification process is dangerous at best. There is a very famous case in the United States involving the prosecution of a Catholic priest, a gentleman named Father Bernard Pagano. He was also called the gentleman bandit. He was accused of a series of robberies, five to be exact. Five separate eye-witnesses, five individuals who pointed out Father Pagano and claimed he was the bandit, he was the man. It was argued that they corroborated each other. Grace be to God and fortune, the true criminal confessed and the case against Father Pagano was dismissed. I trust you will do the same here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I take it this concludes your reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Until tomorrow when we will be dealing with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure. Your reply on the appeal -- on the other appeal here. Well, I believe there is no question from the Bench. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not scheduled to say anything until about 3.30 tomorrow, but may I just, please, say something before Your Honours rise as a matter of courtesy, and it's this: That I gave to Ms. Brady before we started this afternoon, a document that we are familiar to prepare in England for a Court of Appeal, namely, what we would call a skeleton argument outlining in summary form the key submissions that we shall be making for Mr. Musliu. Your Honours, I merely tell you we have done that. We have provided copies for you as well. We recognise or we understand, rather, that that is not necessarily something this Chamber is used to receiving. May I simply indicate that it is there. If Your Honours wish to see it, then of course you will. It may be thought to have the advantage of reducing what I need to say tomorrow, but we leave it in the Court's hands as to whether or not they wish to consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, as you -- I quickly consulted myself, but as you yourself said it's not in practice of this Court to accept submissions, written submissions, at this very late stage. So we appreciate you gave it to the -- your colleagues in the OTP, but we will not make use of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I wonder if I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: -- just raise one other matter; it's not a submission. I have, in fact, provided the Prosecutor, Helen Brady, with this document. It's an attempt to answer your questions in a little detail with references to evidence and so on. I was intending first thing tomorrow to provide you with the document unless, again, it's not something you would normally receive. But as your questions were received very recently and it will save a great deal of court time and as the Prosecutor already has this list, it may need amendment overnight, I just indicate now I'd like to hand it in in the morning to save time, but again I'll be receptive to any guidance you may give. It's a document that stretches to four pages with footnotes, so it's just -- it's just geared to the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I hear the Prosecution on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I haven't had a chance to properly study this document, but I appreciate that counsel has given us the opportunity to do so. We're not planning to file a separate set of answers to your questions; we will be dealing with it in oral submissions. We don't have a problem with this document being filed in answer to the question, especially as it puts out the evidence -- sets out the evidence in some detail, and it may shorten the matter if we could have it in this filed form. I think it's quite different from the document that Mr. Topolski was referring to, so we wouldn't take objection to this particular form in which Mr. Mansfield has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine. So if there is no objection from the Prosecution, we can certainly admit this document when --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- Tomorrow morning, of course, when you will submit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, if there is no other matter we can rise now and meet -- reconvene tomorrow at 9.00 for the appeal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
